expected_points: Adjust the amount of guidance to the team’s experience and trust: give junior team members more detail, and let experienced, trusted people work with less.

sections.heading: How much detail to provide
sections.content: There is no universal level of detail: treat it as a dial that depends on who is on the team. The work should communicate the idea clearly enough that a technical person knows what to build—not just offer a vague sketch—but avoid detailing implementation choices, such as a database schema, in a way that dictates how a senior engineer must do the work. Singer also warns that detailed solutioning without engineering involvement can lead to painful reality checks.

sections.heading: If the engineer wants input
sections.content: Bring the engineer into shaping and work through the technical approach together. Singer describes trying ideas and having the technical person identify what will not work, while product checks whether the technically easy option still delivers customer value. Ideally, involve the person who understands the system and what is feasible or difficult in the infrastructure.

sections.heading: Calibrate the amount of detail
sections.content: Singer says the common failure is too little detail, but the useful level varies by team and is a dial to turn. Avoid prescribing technical specifics—such as how a senior engineer should implement a database schema—when that would overstep. Instead, shape the work until its main moving parts and connections are clear, and a technical person can say they know what to build. A high-level sketch is not enough if it leaves the builder unsure what to make.

answer.summary: Singer says to tune implementation detail to the team: provide enough clarity that an engineer knows what to build, but shape the solution with engineering rather than prescribing technical internals. If an engineer wants input, bring them into shaping to test feasibility and help determine the approach.

sections.heading: Calibrate the amount of detail
sections.content: Treat detail as a dial, not a fixed level: Singer says the amount that helps depends on who is on the team. Avoid specifying technical internals—such as exactly how a senior engineer should implement a database schema—when that would overstep. But don’t leave the work so vague that it is merely a blurry sketch: the shaped idea should communicate what to build, so a technical person can say, “I know what to go build now.”

sections.heading: If the engineer wants input
sections.content: Include the engineer in the shaping work rather than finalizing a detailed solution without them. Singer describes trying out ideas together and asking the technical person to find what will not work, while product checks whether the idea delivers customer value. Ideally, involve the senior engineer who knows the system and what is feasible; use their input to identify the solution’s moving parts and shape an approach the team believes it can finish in the allotted time. This is collaborative feasibility-checking, not handing down a technical recipe.
